claim: GIPC1 forms a domain-swapped dimer.
source: A prominent feature of the GIPC1 structure is that two molecules in the asymmetric unit form a domain-swapped dimer (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by X-ray crystal structure determination at 1.9 Å resolution showing two molecules in the asymmetric unit forming a domain-swapped dimer.

claim: The domain swap in GIPC1 results from an exchange of the last β-strand between the two GH1 domains.
source: The domain swap is the result of an exchange of the last β-strand between the two GH1 domains (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure showing the exchange of the last β-strand.

claim: The GH1 domain adopts an ubiquitin-like fold.
source: The GH1 domain adopts an ubiquitin-like fold composed of four β-strands and one α-helix, although it lacks obvious sequence similarity to ubiquitin (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis showing the fold composition and comparison with ubiquitin.

claim: The GH2 domain forms a four-helix globular fold.
source: The GH2 domain forms a four-helix globular fold (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by structural data from the crystal structure.

claim: The PDZ domain in GIPCs is flanked by a N-terminal GIPC-homology 1 (GH1) domain and a C-terminal GH2 domain.
source: The PDZ domain in GIPCs is flanked by a N-terminal GIPC-homology 1 (GH1) domain and a C-terminal GH2 domain (Katoh, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature and confirmed by structural data.

claim: The structure of the PDZ domain of GIPC1 is similar to that of the isolated PDZ domain of GIPC2.
source: The structure of the PDZ domain of GIPC1 is similar to that of the isolated PDZ domain of GIPC2 (PDB ID: 3GGE), featuring a typical PDZ fold with five β-strands and two α-helices (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by comparison with previously determined structure (PDB ID: 3GGE).

claim: The loop between helices α1 and α2 in the GH2 domain partially occupies the PBM-binding groove in the PDZ domain.
source: Notably, the loop between helices α1 and α2 in the GH2 domain partially occupies the PBM-binding groove in the PDZ domain (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by structural data showing the spatial relationship between GH2 and PDZ domains.

claim: The PDZ domain blocks one face on the GH2 domain that binds myosin VI.
source: Conversely, the PDZ domain blocks one face on the GH2 domain that binds myosin VI (as defined by the structures of the GH2/myosin VI complexes below).
evidence: Supported by comparison of apo-GIPC1 structure with GH2/myosin VI complex structures.

claim: The apo-GIPC1 structure represents an autoinhibited conformation that hinders binding to both PBM-containing cargo proteins and myosin VI.
source: The apo-GIPC1 structure therefore represents an autoinhibited conformation that hinders binding to both PBM-containing cargo proteins and myosin VI.
evidence: Supported by structural data showing mutual blocking of binding sites and functional assays showing enhanced binding upon cargo binding.

claim: The entire PDZ-GH2 linker and GH2 domain of GIPC1 in the PlexinD1cyto/GIPC1 complex are invisible in the electron-density map.
source: The entire PDZ-GH2 linker and GH2 domain of GIPC1 in the PlexinD1cyto/GIPC1 complex are invisible in the electron-density map.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data showing no electron density for these regions.

claim: The GIPC1 protein is intact in crystals of the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex.
source: A gel analysis shows that the GIPC1 protein is intact in crystals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the linker-GH2 domains are present but completely disordered in the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex structure.
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE analysis of dissolved crystals.

claim: Binding of PlexinD1 to GIPC1 is expected to dislodge the GH2 domain from its autoinhibitory interaction with the PDZ domain.
source: Binding of PlexinD1 to GIPC1 is expected to dislodge the GH2 domain from its autoinhibitory interaction with the PDZ domain, rendering the GH2 domain and the PDZ-GH2 linker conformationally flexible in relation to the GH1-PDZ module (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison and the observation that the GH2 domain is disordered in the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex.

claim: PlexinD1 binding releases the autoinhibition in GIPC1, leading to enhanced interaction with myosin VI.
source: As a result, the GH2 domain can more readily interact with myosin VI, which explains the enhanced recruitment of myosin VI by GIPC1 when GIPC1 is bound to cargo proteins as reported previously (Naccache et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by structural data and previous functional studies showing enhanced myosin VI recruitment.

claim: The GH1 and PDZ domains of GIPC1 in the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex form the same domain-swapped dimer as apo-GIPC1.
source: The GH1 and PDZ domains of GIPC1 in the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex are well structured and form the same domain-swapped dimer as apo-GIPC1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison of the two crystal structures.

claim: The curvature of the canoe-shaped dimer is different in the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex compared to apo-GIPC1.
source: The curvature of the canoe-shaped dimer is, however, different in the two structures, suggesting that the dimer interface between the two GH1 domains has a certain degree of plasticity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison showing conformational differences.

claim: The two PlexinD1cyto molecules are placed at the opposite sides of the GIPC1 dimer and do not contact each other.
source: The two PlexinD1cyto molecules are placed at the opposite sides of the GIPC1 dimer and do not contact each other (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by structural data from the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex.

claim: In the apo-PlexinD1cyto structure, the C-terminal tail region constitutes the C-terminal part of the last helix in the GAP domain, except for the last two residues which are disordered.
source: In the apo-PlexinD1cyto structure, the C-terminal tail region (residues 1916–1925) constitutes the C-terminal part of the last helix in the GAP domain, except for the last two residues (Glu1924 and Ala1925) which are disordered (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural data from the apo-PlexinD1cyto crystal structure.

claim: In the PlexinD1cyto/GIPC1 complex, the tail segment adopts an ordered, extended conformation.
source: In contrast, the tail segment in the PlexinD1cyto/GIPC1 complex adopts an ordered, extended conformation (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural data from the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex crystal structure.

claim: The PBM interacts with the PDZ domain in GIPC1 in the typical PBM/PDZ-binding mode.
source: As expected, the PBM interacts with the PDZ domain in GIPC1 in the typical PBM/PDZ-binding mode, where the PBM forms a short β-strand to pack in an anti-parallel fashion with strand β2 in the PDZ domain (Figure 4A) (Ye and Zhang, 2013).
evidence: Supported by structural data and comparison with known PBM/PDZ interactions.

claim: The sidechain of the very C-terminal residue (Ala1925) in the PBM is buried in the hydrophobic pocket between helix α2 and strand β2 of the PDZ domain.
source: The sidechain of the very C-terminal residue (Ala1925) in the PBM is buried in the hydrophobic pocket between helix α2 and strand β2 of the PDZ domain, while its carbonyl group interacts with the backbone atoms of Leu143 and Gly144 in the PDZ domain.
evidence: Supported by structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: GIPC1 makes extensive contacts with other residues in the C-terminal tail as well as the two preceding helices of PlexinD1, resulting in a large interface with the total buried surface area of 2072 Å2.
source: In addition to these canonical PBM/PDZ interactions, GIPC1 makes extensive contacts with other residues in the C-terminal tail as well as the two preceding helices of PlexinD1, resulting in a large interface with the total buried surface area of 2072 Å2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and surface area calculations.

claim: Ile1918 and Y1919 in the tail of PlexinD1 plug into a hydrophobic pocket formed at the junction between the GH1 and PDZ domain.
source: Notably, Ile1918 and Y1919 in the tail of PlexinD1 plug into a hydrophobic pocket formed at the junction between the GH1 and PDZ domain.
evidence: Supported by structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: Most residues involved in the PlexinD1/GIPC1 interactions are highly conserved in PlexinD1 from different species but divergent in other plexin family members.
source: Most residues involved in these interactions are highly conserved in PlexinD1 from different species but divergent in other plexin family members (Figure 4B), supporting the functional relevance of these interactions (Burk et al., 2017; Gay et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis and citations to functional studies.

claim: The additional interactions beyond the canonical PBM/PDZ interface likely enhance the affinity and specificity between PlexinD1 and GIPC1.
source: These additional interactions likely enhance the affinity and specificity between PlexinD1 and GIPC1.
evidence: Supported by structural data showing extensive interactions and comparison with other PDZ/PBM interactions.

claim: The dual binding mode between PlexinD1 and GIPC1 is analogous to the interaction between class B plexins and PDZ-RhoGEF.
source: This dual binding mode is analogous to the interaction between class B plexins and PDZ-RhoGEF where the secondary interface significantly increases the binding affinity (Pascoe et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by comparison with previously reported structure and functional data.

claim: The GH2 domain in apo-GIPC1 sterically clashes with PlexinD1 when superimposed with the PlexinD1/GIPC1 complex.
source: A superimposition of the PlexinD1cyto/GIPC1 complex with apo-GIPC1 shows that the GH2 domain sterically clashes with PlexinD1 (Figure 4C), supporting the notion that the GH2 domain in apo-GIPC1 is autoinhibitory and must dissociate before PlexinD1 can bind.
evidence: Supported by structural superimposition showing steric clashes.

claim: The HCBD of myosin VI adopts the same two-helix conformation as seen in the recent NMR structure (PDB ID: 2N10).
source: The HCBD of myosin VI adopts the same two-helix conformation as seen in the recent NMR structure (PDB ID: 2N10), with the 'RRL' motif located at the center of the second helix (Figure 5B) (He et al., 2016; Wollscheid et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by comparison with previously determined NMR structure.

claim: There are five copies of both myosin VI-HCBD and GIPC1-GH2 molecules in each asymmetric unit, arranged in an alternating pattern.
source: There are five copies of both myosin VI-HCBD and GIPC1-GH2 molecules in each asymmetric unit, arranged in an alternating pattern (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data showing the asymmetric unit composition.

claim: The group of five HCBD and GH2 domains repeats itself in the neighboring unit cell, yielding a continuous array of alternating HCBD and GH2 that extends throughout the crystal.
source: The group of five HCBD and GH2 domains repeats itself in the neighboring unit cell, yielding a continuous array of alternating HCBD and GH2 that extends throughout the crystal (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic analysis of crystal packing.

claim: The neighboring units in the GH2/HCBD array are related roughly by a five-fold right-handed rotational symmetry and a ~22 Å translation.
source: Considering one GH2/HCBD pair as a unit, the neighboring units in the array are related roughly by a five-fold right-handed rotational symmetry and a ~22 Å translation.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic analysis of the repeating unit arrangement.

claim: The GIPC2-GH2/myosin VI structure forms the same alternating array as the GIPC1-GH2/myosin VI structure, despite being crystallized in a different condition and space group.
source: The GIPC2-GH2/myosin VI structure forms the same alternating array, despite being crystallized in a different condition and space group (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data from two independent structures.

claim: The recurrence of the repeating array in two different crystal forms argues strongly that this arrangement captures the oligomeric interaction mode between GIPCs and myosin VI that is relevant to function.
source: The recurrence of this repeating array argues strongly that this arrangement captures the oligomeric interaction mode between GIPCs and myosin VI that is relevant to function, rather than being a crystal packing artifact.
evidence: Supported by observation of the same arrangement in two independent crystal structures and functional considerations.

claim: The oligomer may collect multiple myosin VI molecules to enhance the processive transport of endocytic vesicles on actin filaments.
source: The oligomer may collect multiple myosin VI molecules to enhance the processive transport of endocytic vesicles on actin filaments, as suggested by the observation that multiple myosin VI dimers attached to the same cargo can coordinate their movements to drive long-distance runs over interlaced actin networks (Sivaramakrishnan and Spudich, 2009).
evidence: Supported by structural data and citation to previous functional studies.

claim: High-order oligomerization of GIPC1 and myosin VI may make the clustering of cell surface receptors into clathrin-coated pits more efficient.
source: In such cells, high-order oligomerization of GIPC1 and myosin VI may make this process more efficient.
evidence: Supported by structural data showing oligomerization and functional considerations.

claim: The bivalent interactions between the GIPC-GH2 and myosin VI-HCBD are mediated by two distinct interfaces.
source: The bivalent interactions between the GIPC-GH2 and myosin VI-HCBD are mediated by two distinct interfaces (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by structural data showing two separate binding interfaces.

claim: Interface I involves the two loops in the GIPC-GH2 domain, one between helices α1 and α2 and the other between helices α3 and α4.
source: Interface I involves the two loops in the GIPC-GH2 domain, one between helices α1 and α2 and the other between helices α3 and α4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by structural data showing the specific regions involved in interface I.

claim: Interface I buries ~1300 Å2 solvent accessible surface area.
source: Interfaces I and II bury ~1300 and ~1100 Å2 solvent accessible surface area, respectively.
evidence: Supported by surface area calculations from structural data.

claim: Interface II buries ~1100 Å2 solvent accessible surface area.
source: Interfaces I and II bury ~1300 and ~1100 Å2 solvent accessible surface area, respectively.
evidence: Supported by surface area calculations from structural data.

claim: The two interfaces in the GIPC2-GH2/HCBD complex structure are highly similar to those in the GIPC1-GH2/HCBD complex.
source: The two interfaces in the GIPC2-GH2/HCBD complex structure are highly similar to those in the GIPC1-GH2/HCBD complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison of the two complex structures.

claim: The inter-domain interaction in apo-GIPC1 prevents the loop between helices α1 and α2 in the GH2 domain from forming interface I with HCBD in myosin VI.
source: Conversely, the inter-domain interaction prevents this loop from forming interface I with HCBD in myosin VI (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison showing steric hindrance.

claim: Interface II in the GH2 domain in the autoinhibited structure of GIPC1 is open for interacting with myosin VI.
source: Interface II in the GH2 domain in the autoinhibited structure of GIPC1 is open for interacting with myosin VI.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis showing that interface II is not blocked in the autoinhibited state.

claim: GST-HCBD was able to pull-down GIPC1 but not PlexinD1cyto.
source: As expected, GST-HCBD was able to pull-down GIPC1 but not PlexinD1cyto (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data.

claim: Mixing PlexinD1cyto, GIPC1, and GST-HCBD allowed GST-HCBD to pull-down both GIPC1 and PlexinD1cyto.
source: Mixing the three proteins allowed GST-HCBD to pull-down both GIPC1 and PlexinD1cyto.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data.

claim: The presence of PlexinD1cyto increased the amount of GIPC1 pulled-down by GST-HCBD substantially.
source: Notably, the presence of Plexincyto increased the amount of GIPC1 pulled-down substantially.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data showing increased GIPC1 binding in the presence of PlexinD1.

claim: The enhancement of GIPC2 binding to GST-HCBD caused by PlexinD1 is more pronounced than for GIPC1.
source: The results were similar, except that the enhancement of GIPC2 binding to GST-HCBD caused by PlexinD1 is more pronounced.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data comparing GIPC1 and GIPC2.

claim: Truncation of the three C-terminal residues in the PBM of PlexinD1 (ΔSEA) virtually abolished the interaction with GIPC1.
source: Truncation of the three C-terminal residues in the PBM of PlexinD1 (ΔSEA) virtually abolished the interaction with GIPC1.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data with the PlexinD1 ΔSEA mutant.

claim: Mutating Ile1918 and Tyr1919 in PlexinD1 (I1918A/Y1919A) reduced the binding to GIPC1 substantially.
source: Mutating Ile1918 and Tyr1919 in PlexinD1 (I1918A/Y1919A), which occupy the hydrophobic pocket between GH1 and PDZ in GIPC1 (Figure 4A), reduced the binding to GIPC1 substantially (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data with the PlexinD1 I1918A/Y1919A mutant.

claim: A mutation of Gly114 in GIPC1 (G114Y) reduced the PlexinD1/GIPC1 interaction.
source: Conversely, a mutation of Gly114 in GIPC1 (G114Y), located at the edge of the hydrophobic packet that accommodates the Ile1918/Tyr1919 motif in PlexinD1 (Figure 4A), also reduced the PlexinD1/GIPC1 interaction (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data with the GIPC1 G114Y mutant.

claim: The GIPC1-GH2 domain at 30 μM displayed a standardized sedimentation coefficient (s20,w-value) of ~1.3 S, corresponding to a monomeric species of ~8 kDa.
source: The GIPC1-GH2 domain at 30 μM displayed a standardized sedimentation coefficient (s20,w-value) of ~1.3 S, corresponding to a monomeric species of ~8 kDa (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data.

claim: The s20,w-value of the myosin VI-HCBD (~5 kDa) at 20 μM was 0.9 S, consistent with a monomeric species.
source: The s20,w-value of the myosin VI-HCBD (~5 kDa) at 20 μM was 0.9 S, also consistent with a monomeric species (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data.

claim: When GIPC1-GH2 and myosin VI-HCBD were mixed at a 1:1 molar ratio, the proteins appeared to form multiple complexes.
source: When mixed at a 1:1 molar ratio, the proteins appeared to form multiple complexes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data showing multiple species.

claim: As the overall concentration of the GH2/HCBD complex was increased, the s20,ww also rose, consistent with the formation of higher order species.
source: As the overall concentration was increased, the s20,ww also rose, consistent with the formation of higher order species (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data at different concentrations.

claim: No species with s20,w-values greater than ~4.8 S were observed for the GH2/HCBD complex.
source: However, we observed no species with s20,w-values greater than ~4.8 S (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), and the increase in s20,ww ceased at concentrations higher than 150 μM (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data.

claim: 4.8 S could represent a 5:5 complex between the GH2 and HCBD based on hydrodynamic estimates.
source: Based on hydrodynamic estimates, 4.8 S could represent a 5:5 complex between the GH2 and HCBD.
evidence: Supported by hydrodynamic calculations based on AUC data.

claim: The formation of very long, linear polymers of the GH2/HCBD complex could be inhibited by the pressures induced by ultracentrifugation.
source: One possible explanation for this phenomenon is that the formation of very long, linear polymers could be inhibited by the pressures induced by ultracentrifugation (Harrington and Kegeles, 1973; Marcum and Borisy, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous studies on polymer behavior under centrifugation and inference from the observed data.

claim: Mixing the linker-GH2 and HCBD led to heavy precipitation.
source: Surprisingly, mixing the linker-GH2 and HCBD led to heavy precipitation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by visual observation of precipitation.

claim: The precipitation of the linker-GH2/HCBD complex could be reversed by increasing the salt concentration from 150 mM to 500 mM.
source: The precipitation is unlikely due to denaturation of the proteins, as it could be reversed by increasing the salt concentration from 150 mM to 500 mM.
evidence: Supported by observation that precipitation is reversible with salt addition.

claim: The PDZ-GH2 linker in GIPC1 appears to enhance the oligomerization of the GIPC1/myosin VI complex.
source: These observations, reminiscent of the reversible precipitation of IRE1 due to the high-order oligomerization (Korennykh et al., 2009), suggest that the PDZ-GH2 linker promotes the polymerization of the myosin VI-HCBD/GIPC1-GH2 complex.
evidence: Supported by precipitation behavior and comparison with IRE1 oligomerization.

claim: The linker-GH2 protein sedimented as a monomer at both 38 μM and 200 μM, with a s20,w-value of ~1.4 S.
source: The linker-GH2 protein sedimented as a monomer at both 38 μM and 200 μM, with a s20,w-value value of ~1.4 S (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data.

claim: The HCBD at 150 μM under high salt conditions sedimented predominantly as a monomer (s20,w-value of 0.9 S), and a minor dimer peak (s20,w-value of 1.6 S).
source: The HCBD at 150 μM under the same condition sedimented predominantly as a monomer (s20,w-value of 0.9 S), and a minor dimer peak (s20,w-value of 1.6 S) (Figure 7—figure supplements 1D and 2F).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data.

claim: The average sizes of the linker-GH2/HCBD complex increased as a function of concentration, with the largest observed s20,w-value of ~5.5 S.
source: Similar to the GH2/HCBD complex, the average sizes of the linker-GH2/HCBD complex increased as a function of concentration, with the largest observed s20,w-value of ~5.5 S (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data at different concentrations.

claim: GIPC1-GH2 and myosin VI-HCBD form high-order oligomers in solution.
source: These results together demonstrate that GIPC1-GH2 and myosin VI-HCBD form high-order oligomers in solution, and both interfaces I and II as seen in our crystal structures are required for the oligomerization.
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data and mutational analysis.

claim: Both interfaces I and II as seen in the crystal structures are required for the oligomerization of GIPC1-GH2 and myosin VI-HCBD.
source: These results together demonstrate that GIPC1-GH2 and myosin VI-HCBD form high-order oligomers in solution, and both interfaces I and II as seen in our crystal structures are required for the oligomerization.
evidence: Supported by mutational analysis showing that disruption of either interface reduces oligomerization.

claim: Sema3E/PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI co-localized very well and formed large puncta in cells expressing wild-type PlexinD1.
source: Sema3E/PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI co-localized very well and formed large puncta in cells expressing wild-type PlexinD1 (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy imaging data.

claim: In cells expressing PlexinD1(ΔSEA), GIPC1 and myosin VI formed puncta together, but Sema3E did not localize to these puncta.
source: In cells expressing PlexinD1(ΔSEA), GIPC1 and myosin VI also formed puncta together, but Sema3E did not localize to these puncta (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy imaging data.

claim: There are virtually no large puncta with Sema3E/PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI co-localized in cells expressing PlexinD1(ΔSEA).
source: There is virtually no large puncta with Sema3E/PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI co-localized in these cells.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy imaging data and quantification.

claim: Replacing wild-type GIPC1 with the G323Q mutant abolished formation of large puncta of co-localized Sema3E/PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI.
source: Replacing wild-type GIPC1 with the G323Q mutant, which disrupts interface II in the GH2 domain for myosin VI, also abolished formation of large puncta of co-localized Sema3E/PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy imaging data and quantification.

claim: Sema3E, PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI can form high-order oligomers in cells.
source: These results support the notion that Sema3E, PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI can form high-order oligomers in cells, which is dependent on both the PlexinD1/GIPC1 interaction and the linear oligomerization of the GIPC1/myosin VI complex.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing co-localization and dependence on specific interactions.

claim: The formation of high-order oligomers of Sema3E, PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI in cells is dependent on both the PlexinD1/GIPC1 interaction and the linear oligomerization of the GIPC1/myosin VI complex.
source: These results support the notion that Sema3E, PlexinD1, GIPC1 and myosin VI can form high-order oligomers in cells, which is dependent on both the PlexinD1/GIPC1 interaction and the linear oligomerization of the GIPC1/myosin VI complex.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing that disruption of either interaction abolishes large puncta formation.

claim: GIPC1 and its two paralogs GIPC2 and GIPC3 are universal adaptor proteins that bind and regulate vesicular trafficking of many transmembrane proteins.
source: GIPC1 (GAIP interacting protein, C-terminus 1) and its two paralogs GIPC2 and GIPC3 are universal adaptor proteins that bind and regulate vesicular trafficking of many transmembrane proteins (Katoh, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: GIPCs contribute to the endocytosis process by tethering the cargo proteins on endocytic vesicles to the motor protein myosin VI.
source: GIPCs contribute to the endocytosis process by tethering the cargo proteins on endocytic vesicles to the motor protein myosin VI (Bunn et al., 1999; Naccache et al., 2006; Reed et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin VI is the only known actin-based motor that walks toward the minus/pointed end of actin filaments.
source: Myosin VI is the only known actin-based motor that walks toward the minus/pointed end of actin filaments and therefore is specialized at transporting endocytic vesicles inward from the cell cortex (Spudich and Sivaramakrishnan, 2010; Sweeney and Houdusse, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin VI and GIPCs contribute to earlier steps of endocytosis, including facilitating the formation of clathrin-coated pits and clustering ligand-bound cell surface receptors into the pits.
source: Myosin VI and GIPCs also contribute to earlier steps of endocytosis, including facilitating the formation of clathrin-coated pits and clustering ligand-bound cell surface receptors into the pits (Hasson, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The GIPC/myosin VI complex acts as an anchor on the cell surface, which is critical for maintaining the structural integrity of stereocilia in the inner ear.
source: Another function of the GIPC/myosin VI complex is to act as an anchor on the cell surface. This function is critical for maintaining the structural integrity of stereocilia in the inner ear, and many mutations of GIPC3 or myosin VI have been found to cause familial hearing loss (Katoh, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: Many mutations of GIPC3 or myosin VI have been found to cause familial hearing loss.
source: This function is critical for maintaining the structural integrity of stereocilia in the inner ear, and many mutations of GIPC3 or myosin VI have been found to cause familial hearing loss (Katoh, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: GIPCs contain a central PDZ domain that mediates the interaction with the C-terminal PDZ-binding motif (PBM) in cargo proteins.
source: GIPCs contain a central PDZ (PSD-95, Dlg and ZO-1) domain that mediates the interaction with the C-terminal PDZ-binding motif (PBM) in cargo proteins.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of GIPC structure and function.

claim: The GH1 and PDZ domains together mediate oligomerization of GIPCs.
source: The GH1 and PDZ domains together mediate oligomerization of GIPCs (Bunn et al., 1999; Gao et al., 2000; Jeanneteau et al., 2004; Kedlaya et al., 2006; Reed et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The GH2 domain mediates the interaction with myosin VI.
source: The GH2 domain mediates the interaction with myosin VI (Naccache et al., 2006; Reed et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cargo binding to the PDZ domain in GIPC1 promotes the interaction with myosin VI.
source: Cargo binding to the PDZ domain in GIPC1 promotes the interaction with myosin VI, suggesting that the two binding events in GIPCs are regulated and communicate with each other through a steric or allosteric mechanism (Naccache et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The motor activity of myosin VI is normally suppressed by autoinhibition.
source: The motor activity of myosin VI is normally suppressed by autoinhibition, which can be released by binding of adaptor proteins through a mechanism that is poorly understood (French et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: An 'RRL' motif between the coiled-coil and CBD in myosin VI is critical for binding to GIPCs.
source: An 'RRL' (single-letter amino acid code) motif between the coiled-coil and CBD in myosin VI is critical for binding to GIPCs (He et al., 2016; Spudich et al., 2007; Wollscheid et al., 2016), but the mode of the interaction was unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Processive walking of myosin VI along actin filaments requires its dimerization.
source: Processive walking of myosin VI along actin filaments requires its dimerization, mediated by both the coiled-coil and binding of adaptor proteins (Masters and Buss, 2017; Park et al., 2006; Phichith et al., 2009; Spudich et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Larger oligomers of myosin VI have been implicated in coordinated long-distance runs over dense and interlaced actin networks.
source: Larger oligomers of myosin VI have been implicated in coordinated long-distance runs over dense and interlaced actin networks (Sivaramakrishnan and Spudich, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PlexinD1 contains a C-terminal 'SEA' motif that constitutes a PBM and interacts with GIPC1.
source: The transmembrane receptor PlexinD1 contains a C-terminal 'SEA' motif that constitutes a PBM and interacts with GIPC1 (Gay et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Semaphorin binding induces the formation of the active dimer of plexin.
source: Semaphorin binding induces the formation of the active dimer of plexin (Janssen et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dimerization of plexin activates the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain in the plexin cytoplasmic region.
source: The dimerization activates the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain in the plexin cytoplasmic region (referred to as plexincyto thereafter), which transduces the signal by switching off the small GTPase Rap (He et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Semaphorin-stimulated endocytosis of plexin contributes to the repulsive guidance function.
source: Semaphorin-stimulated endocytosis of plexin contributes to the repulsive guidance function (Fournier et al., 2000; Tojima et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GIPC1-mediated endocytic trafficking and sorting of Sema3E-activated PlexinD1 play important regulatory roles in PlexinD1 signaling.
source: A recent study has shown that GIPC1-mediated endocytic trafficking and sorting of Sema3E-activated PlexinD1 play important regulatory roles in PlexinD1 signaling (Burk et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.

claim: The high degree of sequence similarity in the GIPC family suggests that GIPC2 and GIPC3 also form similar domain-swapped dimers.
source: The high degree of sequence similarity in the GIPC family suggests that GIPC2 and GIPC3 also form similar domain-swapped dimers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis and structural similarity.

claim: The autoinhibited structure of GIPC1 represents a conserved regulation mechanism of the GIPC family.
source: These results support the notion that the autoinhibited structure of GIPC1 represents a conserved regulation mechanism of the GIPC family.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assays showing similar behavior for GIPC1, GIPC2, and GIPC3.

claim: The alternating array of GH2 and HCBD underlies the oligomerization of the GIPC/Myosin VI complexes in solution and cells.
source: Our data support that this alternating array underlies the oligomerization of the GIPC/Myosin VI complexes in solution and cells.
evidence: Supported by crystal structures, AUC data, and cell imaging data.
